zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Supplied page subset; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The scan remains the authority for text and typography.

lines.note: Imi denotes a taboo or ominous restriction. Connichi imiga aita says that the restriction ended today; the scan supports g rather than OCR q and a full stop after aita, not a continuation hyphen.

runs.text: Oje ſe acabou o agouro, ou prohibição de ir a

lines.note: The Portuguese explains that the taboo or prohibition against going somewhere ended today. Oje is the historical spelling, not a reason to insert modern initial h.

runs.text: algũa parte ou fazer algũa couſa.

lines.note: The continuation adds going to a place or doing something. Both occurrences of algũa retain their abbreviated nasal rather than being expanded.

runs.text: Obra, ou ceremonia q̃ ſe faz por agouro.

lines.note: Imigoto is a deed or ceremony performed because of a taboo or omen. The scan restores the missing i in the headword and reads Obra, ou, not the OCR's cou.
Imijij here means fortunate or blessed. Quafô imijij fi-to describes a fortunate person; the Japanese spelling and the circumflex on Quafô remain distinct from modern forms.
To completes fito, followed by "a fortunate and blessed man." The physical division fi-to is preserved.

Imijiſa and Imijǔ are derivatives of the preceding adjective. The far-right agouro belongs logically to Imimono on the next row; its faint preceding parenthesis is retained from the surviving stroke and the clearer parallel in c1-l022.

runs.text: Couſa de q̃ ſe tem aſco ou ſetoma por

lines.note: Imimono is something regarded with aversion or as ominous. The definition ends with por here and is completed by the displaced agouro physically above, not by a missing new line.

runs.text: Rego por onde corre agoa pera as

lines.note: Imizo denotes an irrigation channel carrying water toward cultivated lowlands. The historical agoa and pera are retained instead of modernized spellings.
Varzeas completes the destination of the irrigation water. This is a short continuation of Imizo, not an independent geographical entry.
Imo is glossed Inhame, a yam-like tuber. The initial I is visible and corrects OCR lowercase l; the gloss does not justify a more precise modern species identification.
This homonymous Imo is a poetic term for a woman or wife. P. marks poetic usage, and the historical Portuguese Molher is preserved.
Imoji, alternatively imonoxe, is a founder of vessels. The alternative is part of the headword apparatus, while the material specification continues below.
The vessels are made of iron or bronze. Bronzo is the printed historical form and is not silently replaced by modern bronze.

runs.text: Hum comer que ſe faz de inhames

lines.note: Imomaqi is a prepared food made from yams. The Portuguese verb is faz, with f, not the OCR's ſaz; the description continues with how the yams are prepared.

runs.text: ralados feitos em Xiru como polme.

lines.note: The yams are grated and made into Xiru with a batter-like consistency. Xiru is Japanese embedded in the Portuguese explanation; the scan prints the whole word in the surrounding italic type.

runs.text: Certo bicho aßi chamado que ſe cria

lines.note: Imomuxi is described as a creature that develops in yams. The gloss supports the caterpillar/grub sense without requiring assignment to a particular species.
Nos inhames completes the habitat or food-plant description. Its relation to Imomuxi above is retained as a separate physical row.
Imonoxe is equated with Imoji and directs the reader upward. Imoji is a Japanese synonym after i, not an embedded Portuguese term requiring a typeface toggle.

runs.text: Hum bicho como oſga, ou lagartixa

lines.note: Imori denotes the creature compared with a gecko or small lizard. The Portuguese is a historical descriptive comparison, not a modern taxonomic classification.
Peçonhenta completes the description as poisonous. This qualification belongs to the preceding animal entry and is preserved as the source's claim.

Imoto means a younger sister. Irmaã retains the clear tilde on the second a; the additional far-right parenthesis and moça complete the following Imotomuco gloss and are preserved as displaced material.
Imotomuco is the brother-in-law married to one's younger sister. Its final moça is physically above at c1-l022; the printed jrmaã is retained rather than modernizing its initial letter.
Imoxe is a poetic expression for husband and wife, equated with Fùfu. The grave on the first u belongs to the Japanese form, not to the Portuguese apparatus.
The scan reads In. Cague., not OCR ſu. Cague means "shade," whereas the Portuguese here explains a temple or monastery; this juxtaposition is retained without repairing the source's mismatch.

runs.text: ſe vſa com algũa compoſiçaõ. Vt,

lines.note: The entry says that In is usually compounded and gives Innai. The two n letters are visible; the stale Ianai hint would obscure the intended "inside the temple" example.

runs.text: tro da Tera, ou do circuito da Tera. Itẽ he pa-

lines.note: Tro completes Dẽtro. The explanation means inside a Tera or its precinct, then starts another use in names; the embedded Tera occurs twice on this row.

runs.text: laura de nomes de caſas, ou familias, & tam

lines.note: The explanation concerns names of houses or families. Tam continues below as bem, without an inferred terminal hyphen.

runs.text: bem de gente dalta familia: ordinaria mente ſe

lines.note: Bem completes tambem, adding persons of high family. Ordinaria mente is visibly separated and remains so in the diplomatic text.

runs.text: uſa no cabo da compoſiçaõ. Vt,

lines.note: The element is generally used at the end of a compound. Qenrei begins the example name Qenrei mon in across the physical break.
Mon in completes the example name, illustrating final in. The printed separation remains intact rather than being joined according to modern spelling.

runs.text: Palaura de liuros que ſe toma, ou por ſom-

lines.note: This In is a bookish term with several senses, beginning with shade. The capital I is restored from the scan, and ſom- continues as bra below.
Bra completes sombra; humidity and autumn are added as further senses or associations. This is the shade/yin entry, distinct from the temple-name discussion above.
In is equated with Voxite and defined as a seal or signet. The first example divides atayuru as ata-yuru; Vt has no added punctuation beyond what the scan supplies.
Yuru completes the verb "give," translating as giving one's seal or sign. The paragraph sign introduces a second expression involving setting or stamping a seal.
In uo ſuyuru, alternatively voſu, means affixing the seal or mark. The historical suyuru is not regularized to a modern verb form.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Piſada, ou raſto de aues. Vt,

lines.note: A further sense is a bird's footprint or track. Xatǒ begins an example about gulls leaving marks in the sand, not a new headword.
The Japanese describes gulls engraving footprints on sandy shore. Qizamu is the verb, and camome is the bird; the Portuguese translation begins with Gaiuotas.

runs.text: que deixaõ raſto dos pès na area da praya.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the description of footprints left in beach sand. The tilde remains on the final o of deixaõ, and pès retains its visible grave.
This In is glossed as human semen. The Japanese paraphrase is printed Vru uǒ with separation; it is retained without forcing the generated kana hint into a new canonical spelling.

Moraſu completes the first expression for emitting semen. Ij in- starts a second example about self-induced emission; its printed spacing and letters are retained rather than interpreted as ordinary modern ii, "good."
The second example is explained as causing an emission oneself. The source's historical polluçaõ and joined porſi remain unmodernized.
Ina is a river-fish name. The brief gloss supplies no secure basis for a narrower species identification in the transcription note.
Another Ina is the negative particle, glossed "no." The scan has i, rather than the OCR's i. before Não.

runs.text: Arroz que eſtà inda nas varze

lines.note: Inaba is marked poetic and denotes rice still standing in the lowland fields. The Portuguese reads Arroz que eſtà inda, correcting several OCR errors; varze continues at the top of column 2.

runs.text: as ja eſpigado. ¶ Item, Alicubi, Lugar al-

lines.note: As completes varzeas from column 1, with rice already in ear. A restricted regional sense follows: a raised place in the field; Lugar begins with a visible capital L lost by OCR.

runs.text: to que fazem no campo onde poem o arroz jũ-

lines.note: To completes alto. The description concerns a raised structure on which rice is placed, with jũ- continuing the Portuguese word juntamente below.

runs.text: tamente com a palha ſobre hũs paos.

lines.note: The rice is placed together with its straw on wooden poles. This completes the regional Inaba definition, not a new entry.

runs.text: Esteira de palha großa. No Ximo ſe

lines.note: Inabaqi is a coarse straw mat. The explanation begins a comparison with Ximo usage; the printed großa and provisional Esteira spelling are retained.
The regional equivalent is Inamaqi. It is embedded after the Portuguese diz and belongs to the same explanation, not to a separate independent entry here.
Inabicari means lightning. The scan's historical Portuguese Relampago is retained without adding a modern accent.

runs.text: Aldea, ou lugares fora dalgũa villa,

lines.note: Inaca denotes a village or places outside a substantial town. The definition continues with a broader regional distinction on the following row.

runs.text: ou cidade principal. Gèralmente fora do Goqi

lines.note: The explanation extends the term to places outside the Goqinai region. The geographical name is embedded in Portuguese and divided physically as Goqi-nai without a printed terminal hyphen.
Nai completes Goqinai, after which the explanation says such places are called Inaca. Neither the fragment nor Inaca is a new headword on this continuation row.
Inacabito denotes a villager or country person. The gloss Aldeão directly supports the person-denoting compound.
Inacazzuto is a gift from the countryside or a village. The doubled z is part of the historical Japanese spelling, not a duplicated OCR character to simplify.
Inacǒdo is another country-person term. The damaged c and caron are retained from the scan, without normalizing the contracted headword to Inacabito.

runs.text: Couſa de que ſe hũ eſpanta.

lines.note: Inacoto is something that surprises a person. Hũ is the abbreviated Portuguese hum; it is not part of the Japanese headword.

runs.text: P. i, Flor, ou erua que nace en-

lines.note: Inadeguſa is a poetic term for a flower or herb growing among rice. The Portuguese reads erua, not OCR crua, and en- continues below.
Tre completes entre, specifying growth among the rice. This continuation should not be detached from the plant description.
Inago denotes grasshoppers. The Portuguese plural does not require plural marking in the Japanese headword.

runs.text: Rostolho que fica depois do arroz

lines.note: Inaguqi is the stubble remaining after rice is cut. Rostolho is retained as printed, including the provisional st classification.
Segado completes the description of harvested rice. The initial long s is retained rather than confused with f.

runs.text: Cileiro de guardar arroz cõ eſpiga.

lines.note: Inagura is a granary for storing rice still in the ear. The scan prints Cileiro, a historical spelling not to be silently replaced by celeiro.
Inamaqi refers the reader back to Inabaqi, the straw-mat entry. The latter is a cross-reference in the explanatory apparatus.

runs.text: Modo de ſe ondear com o vento o

lines.note: Inamuxiro describes the rice crop's wave-like motion in wind. The apparent mat metaphor is explained by the following comparison rather than treated as a literal mat here.

runs.text: arroz em erua, ou eſpigado inclinandoſe todo a

lines.note: The rice, green or already in ear, bends together. Inclinandoſe retains its joined reflexive form and long s.
The crop leans to one side like a mat. Inamuxiroga begins the illustrated verbal expression on this row.

runs.text: Fazerem ſe estas ondas no arroz.

lines.note: Suru completes the expression for the rice making these waves. The final upright P. marks poetic usage, not part of the italic translation.

runs.text: Maneira de ondas q̃ com o vento ſe

lines.note: Inanami likewise describes waves produced by the wind in rice fields. The abbreviated q̃ belongs to the Portuguese relative clause.

runs.text: fazem no arroz que està nas varzeas.

lines.note: The waves form in rice still standing in the lowland fields. The closing P. is the poetry label and is retained in roman type.
Inanaqi gives principal forms for a horse's neighing. The Portuguese preference marker begins Me- and continues below; the Japanese forms are not modernized.
Liùs completes Meliùs and recommends Ibai with its principal forms. The scan supplies the missing u and its grave, rather than the OCR's lis.

runs.text: Fazer ir, ou tornar a al-

lines.note: Inaxe means making someone go or return. The dictionary prints ſuru as a principal form here; it is not changed merely to fit a modern conjugation.
Guem completes alguem. The example requests that someone be sent home quickly, with Chachatto and the historical vchiye retained.

runs.text: Peço vos que o façais tor

lines.note: Tamǒre completes the request. Mon. is an upright citation label; the Portuguese reads façais with a visible cedilla, while tor continues without an invented hyphen.
Nar completes tornar, followed by the instruction to return home quickly. The historical de preßa and pera remain unchanged.
Inazzuma denotes lightning. The following Japanese example begins the construction Inazzumaga suru, with doubled z retained.
Suru completes the lightning expression, translated by Relampaguear. Reinspection confirms a small terminal full stop; it is not omitted merely because it is faint in the first overview.
Inban is a seal or signet. The example prints Inbãuo with a nasal-abbreviation tilde over a, not the OCR's unmarked Inbauo.
Qu completes tçuqu in the seal-impression example, with voſu as an alternative. The Portuguese explains putting a seal or mark on something.
Inbô is equated with Mufon, a scheme or plot. The visible f corrects OCR Muron; the gloss about secret treachery supports this Japanese identification.

runs.text: faz eſcondidamente pera armar algũa traição.

lines.note: The scheme is made secretly to contrive treachery. The scan separates faz eſcondidamente; the OCR's joined word obscured that boundary.
Inbon is defined in the source's religious language as a sexual sin. The Japanese example begins the expression for committing it.
Vocaſu completes "commit this sin." The printed long s belongs to the historical Japanese verb and is not replaced by f.
Inbut is a gift or offering. The final t represents the historical checked ending; Inbutuo begins the example with its object particle attached.

Tçucauaſu completes the expression for sending a gift. The worn first vowel of Mandar is read as a from surviving type and bilingual context; the damaged impression is noted rather than passed off as perfectly clear.

Inca is a certificate of a master's approval. The paraphrase is read Yuruxiuo daſaruru; the first u is abraded but compatible with the surviving stroke, whereas OCR Yaruxiuo gives an implausible Japanese form.

runs.text: ção, ou certidão que ſedá dalgum meſtre ao diſ-

lines.note: Ção completes examinação and begins the certification explanation. The scan's ſedá is joined and has an acute accent, not the OCR's nasal tilde; the next word continues as diſ-cipulo.

runs.text: cipulo em que o aproua, & dà por ſufficiente.

lines.note: Cipulo completes the pupil reference. The certificate approves the pupil and declares sufficient competence; the source's ſufficiente is retained.
The paragraph sign, omitted by OCR, introduces Incauo daſu or toru: issuing or receiving the certificate. The paired verbs are a Japanese example, not additional independent headwords.
The Portuguese closes the example as giving or taking this certificate or letter. The centered material below is a quire signature, not a catchword or continuation of the sentence.
